Sunday. Lalit showed Suraj the clip on the school bus: Lalit on his scooter, arguing with a traffic constable, filming it himself. "You can't stop me, I know my rights!" Twelve thousand views. Suraj laughed with everyone, but his chest buzzed. He wanted that too, the likes, the looks in the corridor.

Wednesday. A checkpoint near the flyover. A constable waved Suraj's cousin's scooter over, and Suraj was riding pillion. His hand drifted to his phone. He could film. He could say something smart. Then he saw the constable's tired face and the queue of cars, and thought: this isn't a stage. He took his hand away and handed over the licence when asked. Two minutes, and they were waved on.

The next Monday. Lalit wasn't on the bus. His scooter had been seized after another argument, and his father had been called to the station. The clip was still up. Lalit wasn't laughing about it anymore.

Ojas, I saw that video you were laughing at, the boy shouting at the policeman. Sit. Your Sarita Mausi has a story.

When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, my friend Rani was the bravest girl we knew. One evening a constable stopped a group of us near the lake for being out after dark. Rani put her hands on her hips and said, "Who are you to stop us? Do you know who my father is?" All of us giggled. I felt the pull to say something clever too, to be as bold as her.

I didn't. I don't know why. Maybe because my hands were shaking. I just said, "Sorry, sir, we are going home," and gave my name.

The constable let the rest of us go. Rani, he took to the chowki and called her father. She sat there till ten, crying.

Real courage that night was keeping quiet and getting everyone home. I learned that from my shaking hands.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sarita choosing to apologise and give her name instead of copying Rani was the turning point, because it got her home safely while Rani was taken to the chowki.

qa.a: Rani was probably frightened and ashamed, sitting there till ten and crying after her bold words backfired.

After the bus-stand theft in Changanassery, the police had questioned Jomon for an hour because he'd been standing near the stolen bag. He'd done nothing. But when his Amma came to pick him up from the station, her face was grey.

From that night, the rules changed. Home by six. No evening football. Phone checked at dinner.

"Amma, this is too much!" Jomon burst out on Thursday. "I didn't do anything!"

His mother put down the fish she was cleaning. "I know you didn't. But I sat outside that station for an hour not knowing what was happening to you." Her voice broke.

Jomon went quiet. He hadn't thought about her side of the hour.

That evening he told her everything, the questions, who he'd been with, how Hafsa's brother had vouched for him. Then he offered, "What if I share my location when I'm out, and message when I leave football? Home by seven?"

His Amma thought about it. "Seven. And you message."

Elif had been at the shopping centre in Berlin with her friend Fatima when security stopped them and called the police. Someone had seen two girls in hoodies take headphones from a shop. It wasn't them, and the camera footage proved it within the hour. But her mother had to come and sign for her.

The next week, her mother wouldn't let her go anywhere except school. "No shopping centre. No Fatima's house. Nothing."

Elif felt furious and ashamed at once. She slammed her door. Then, through it, she heard her mother on the phone to her aunt in Turkish, crying. "I thought they would take her away."

Elif sat on the floor for a long time. Then she went to the kitchen.

"Anne, I'm sorry you were scared. Can I tell you everything that happened, from the start?" She did. Afterwards she said, "What if I share my location with you whenever I'm out, and I'm home by eight?"

Her mother wiped her eyes. "Eight. And you answer when I call."

"Ira, aarti time," Nani called from the prayer corner.

Ira put down her phone and went. Her cousin Neelam, visiting for the holidays, followed, smirking.

Afterwards, on the terrace, Neelam said, "You know you don't believe that stuff. You told me last month. So why do you sit there every evening like a good girl?"

"Because Nani likes it when I sit with her."

"But it's fake if you don't believe."

Ira thought. "I don't think the lamp does anything. I've stopped thinking that. But Nani's hands shake now when she holds the plate. She sings off-key and she doesn't care. Sitting there is how I'm with her."

"So you're pretending."

"I'm not pretending to believe. If she asks, I'll tell her. I'm just not going to make fun of something that holds her up."

Neelam was quiet. Then, "Can I sit with you both tomorrow?"

"Only if you don't laugh."

Every Thursday evening, my Ammamma walks to the small Sai temple at the end of our street in Chennai, and every Thursday, I go with her. I'm Urmila, and somewhere in Class 10 I stopped believing most of it.

It didn't happen in one day. I just started finding the rituals empty: the coconut, the bell, the same prayer every week. Once, my friend Mehak asked me, "If you don't believe, why go? Isn't that fake?"

I thought about it for days. Then I realised: I go for Ammamma. She holds my arm on the uneven road. She tells me which aunty's son got married. Inside, she closes her eyes and her face goes soft in a way I never see at home.

I don't fold my hands the way she does anymore. I don't pretend when she asks what I prayed for; I say, "For you, Ammamma." That's true.

And I never, ever laugh at her. It isn't mine to take away.

qa.a: Ammamma walks to the small Sai temple at the end of the street.

qa.q: What does Urmila feel while walking with Ammamma?
qa.a: Urmila feels a warm, protective affection for Ammamma, even though the rituals now feel empty.

qa.q: How does Urmila stay honest while still honouring Ammamma?

Temple kitchen volunteer coordinator's note, Sunday seva

Uma has been coming to the Sunday kitchen every week since she was twelve. She stirs the sambar pot, knows every volunteer aunty by name, and this year she brought her school friend Zainab, who now chops vegetables beside her. The two of them laugh the whole morning.

Today, after serving, Uma asked the priest why only men could carry the deity in procession. A few people looked uneasy. The priest answered calmly, as far as he could. Uma listened and nodded. Later she told me, "I love it here. It feels like home. But I also want to understand the reasons, not just follow."

She seemed worried that asking made her a bad devotee. I told her many people here have asked questions over the years, and still come. The kitchen is not only for people who never ask anything.

She went back and washed the big vessels with Zainab until two. I have asked the priest if the youth group could hold a question session next month.

Sunday, 9 pm

Langar seva again today. I love Sundays at the gurdwara. Vishal and I did the roti line for three hours, flour up to our elbows, and Bebe ji from the next street kept slipping us extra kheer. It's the one place where everyone knows me since I was a baby.

But today I asked Granthi ji something I've been thinking about for months, why some families still sit apart even though the Guru taught equality. My voice shook. I was sure he'd be annoyed.

He wasn't. He said, "Good. The Guru asked questions too," and told me about a book I could read.

On the way home Vishal said, "Weren't you scared?" I was. I'm always scared someone will say asking means I don't belong. But I think I can have both, the roti line and the questions. They don't cancel each other out.

— Urmila

Saturday night

I asked one question at the satsang today, and now half the aunties won't look at me.

We were reading the story of the goddess, and I asked, "Do we believe this happened, or is it a way of teaching?" I really wanted to know. Mala aunty said, loudly, "Such disrespect. This is what English schools do." After that nobody passed me the prasad plate. I sat there with my face burning. On the way out, two of them turned away.

I cried in the auto. I felt like they'd thrown me out of something I've belonged to since I was small.

I called Elizabeth. She listened for a long time. Then she said, "At my church there are people like that, and people who love questions. Don't let the loudest ones be the whole thing."

That made me think of Padma paati, who runs the Tuesday study group and always says, "Ask, ask." I'm going to ask her tomorrow.

Sangeeta

"You're not coming to the prayer meeting?" Hemant stood in the doorway, dressed in white.

Gargi didn't look up from the bed. "No."

"It's for Dadu, Gargi."

"I know who it's for." Her voice cracked. "He prayed every single morning for sixty years. Every morning, bhaiya. And God let him get sick anyway, and let him go in three weeks. So what was the point?"

"I'm so angry," she said. "At God. Is that even allowed?"

Gargi looked up. "He did?"

She cried then, properly. After a while she said, "Can I come and just sit at the back?"

"Of course."

When my dog Bruno died in Class 9, I stopped saying my prayers at night. I'm Varun. I know people lose parents and siblings, and a dog seems small next to that. But he'd slept at the foot of my bed for eleven years.

I remember lying awake thinking, if God is real, why would He let something so good die so slowly? I was angry in a way I'd never been. I felt guilty for being angry, too.

Zeenat, who sits next to me, noticed I was off. When I finally told her, I expected her to be shocked. She wasn't. She said, "After my Abbu's surgery went wrong, I was furious with Allah for months. I still prayed, but I shouted in my head."

It surprised me that someone who believes so much could be so angry.

So I started writing it down instead. Pages of it, just talking to God, or maybe to nobody. I still don't know which. But writing it helped more than staying silent.

Chandrika's mother ran a small dental clinic above the pharmacy, and on Saturdays after six it was the quietest place Chandrika knew. Her father came to pick them up, and her younger brother Hrithik was downstairs buying chips.

She had planned this for weeks. Not during a festival. Not after a fight.

"Mumma, Papa, can I tell you something while we're alone?" Her hands were cold. "I don't believe the way you do anymore. About God, about the pujas. I've been feeling it for a year."

Her mother put down the tray of instruments. Her father sat heavily on the patient's chair.

"I'm not saying you're wrong," Chandrika went on quickly. "I love how Nani's stories matter to you. I respect it. I just don't want to lie to you about me."

Silence. Then her father said, "We need time."

"I know. You don't have to say anything now."

Hrithik's footsteps came up the stairs. Her mother touched her cheek, briefly, before the door opened.

I'm writing this because every time I try to say it out loud, I freeze or it comes out wrong. Ankita helped me find the words, but they're mine.

Navratri, night 5

Everyone went to the pandal again. I said I had a headache. Tanuja texted, "garba??" and I said no. I'm not unwell. I just don't believe any of it, and sitting through the aarti feeling nothing makes me feel like a ghost.

I think I'm the only one in my family who doesn't believe in God. Maybe in the whole colony. That feels so lonely I can't explain it.

So I went up to the terrace. Power cut in half the lane, so the sky was actually dark. I lay on the mat and saw more stars than I ever have in the city. I felt tiny, and it didn't feel bad. It felt huge and quiet. Is that awe? Can I have that without a god?

I wrote down what I actually believe in: honesty, being kind to Dadi, not wasting food, telling the truth even when it's awkward. That's a list. That's something.

Tomorrow I'll tell Tanuja. Maybe she won't laugh.

— Damini

passage:
In the girls' hostel of their Bengaluru college, Parul and Neelam had been roommates for two months before they asked each other the real questions.

It started in Lent. Neelam wasn't eating meat and had given up sweets too. Parul, who fasted every Navratri, was curious. "Why sweets?"

"It's about giving up something you like, to make room for prayer," Neelam said. "Why do you fast?"

Parul thought. "Honestly, part of it is habit. But when I do it properly, it makes me grateful for food."

That became their thing. Late at night, lights off, they'd ask. Parul asked about confession. Neelam asked why Parul's family prayed to so many forms of God. Once, Parul caught herself about to say, "But that doesn't make sense." She stopped and asked, "What does it mean to you?" instead.

Neither of them was trying to win. Neither was trying to change the other. On Neelam's birthday, Parul gave her a small wooden cross from the market. Neelam cried.

qa.q: What did Neelam give up during Lent besides meat?
qa.a: Neelam gave up sweets too.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she asked about the fast?
qa.a: Parul felt curious and interested, wanting to understand Neelam's reasons.

qa.q: What did Parul do that showed listening to learn?
qa.a: Parul stopped herself from saying "that doesn't make sense" and asked what it meant to Neelam instead.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel receiving the wooden cross?
qa.a: Neelam likely felt deeply touched and respected, seeing that Parul honoured her faith without trying to change it.

grounding: It shows two friends of different religions asking each other real questions to learn rather than win, with curiosity and kindness instead of converting.

passage:
Hi Irawati,

It's been a month since you moved to Pune and I miss our walks home. I've been thinking about all the questions we asked each other this year.

Remember when you asked me in Ramzan how I could go all day without even water? And I asked why your family does puja for the tulsi plant? We both laughed at first, and then we actually listened.

I still think about what you said when I told you about sehri at four in the morning. You said, "That sounds hard and kind of beautiful." Nobody had ever said that.

And your Dadi explaining the tulsi to me, how it's like a member of the family, made me see our own neem tree differently.

I never wanted to convince you of anything, and you never tried to convince me. I think that's why it worked. We were just curious, and kind.

Ammi says come for Eid. Please come.

Wasim

qa.q: What time does sehri happen, according to Wasim?
qa.a: Sehri happens at four in the morning.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Irawati called sehri hard and kind of beautiful?
qa.a: Wasim felt touched and understood, since nobody had ever described it that way before.

qa.q: Why did Wasim and Irawati's questions work so well?
qa.a: They asked out of curiosity and listened to learn, without trying to convince each other, so their kindness made the questions safe.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Irawati would likely feel warm and missed, and glad that their questions mattered so much to Wasim. 🙂

grounding: It shows two friends of different religions asking each other real questions, listening to learn, and valuing curiosity and kindness over converting.
